blend-window-sky.start: Start at the top left corner of the canvas, where the window view begins, with Pale sky blue across the very top.
blend-window-sky.strokes: Stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up Titanium white and paint below the blue, then stroke back up over the join while both are wet.
blend-window-sky.inside: The clear blue sits along the top edge, where the sky is deepest; it softens to near white lower down, as sky does near the trees.
blend-window-sky.leave: Leave a few soft white holes along the left edge of the patch for clouds, and keep the rest of the canvas bare white.
blend-window-sky.stop: Stop when the patch is about 3 1/4 in wide and 3 3/4 in tall, with no hard line where the blue meets the white.

dab-dark-leaves.first: Let the sky be dry, so the green taps stay clean instead of turning muddy.
dab-dark-leaves.start: Tap where the sky turns pale low in the window view; the middle of the leaves is about 1 in from the left edge and 1 1/4 in from the top edge.
dab-dark-leaves.strokes: Wipe most of the paint off, then tap straight down with the brush tip; never drag it.
dab-dark-leaves.inside: Keep it to a few light taps low in the window view, where the far trees will grow up from.
dab-dark-leaves.leave: Leave the blue sky and its white cloud holes showing all around the taps.
dab-dark-leaves.stop: Stop while it is only a small, soft cluster of dots. Blobs mean the brush is too wet: wipe it on a paper towel.

dab-pale-leaves.first: Let the green taps from step 2 dry first.
dab-pale-leaves.start: Tap the first pale dot on top of the green taps from step 2, about 1 1/4 in from the left edge.
dab-pale-leaves.strokes: Tap with the tip of a nearly dry brush, a few times in one spot, then lift away.
dab-pale-leaves.inside: The pale taps go on the upper, sunlit side of the green, because the light comes from the upper left.
dab-pale-leaves.leave: Leave some of the darker green taps from step 2 showing underneath, and all the sky around them.
dab-pale-leaves.stop: Stop after a few small taps: this is a light touch, not a new patch of leaves.

blend-wall.first: Let the window view dry before the wall goes in beside it.
blend-wall.start: Start at the top edge just right of the sky through the window, with Pale wall blue, and work across toward the right edge.
blend-wall.strokes: Make short crossing strokes in two directions, like overlapping X shapes, picking up Wall blue as you move across and up.
blend-wall.inside: Keep the paler blue close to the window, where the light falls, and the deeper blue toward the right edge and the top edge.
blend-wall.leave: Leave the bottom of the canvas bare; the wall's lower edge sits about 6 in from the bottom edge and slopes down gently toward the right edge.
blend-wall.stop: Stop when the wall reaches the left, right and top edges as one soft criss-cross blue, with no cat or blanket on it yet.

block-in-frame.first: Let the wall and the window view dry, so the white stays clean.
block-in-frame.start: Start with the wide upright post where the window view meets the wall, pulling it down from the top edge.
block-in-frame.strokes: Build the frame from straight pieces: the wide post, a thinner upright, a crossbar across the upper view, then the wide ledge along the bottom of the window.
block-in-frame.inside: The whole frame is flat white for now; its middle is about 1 3/4 in from the left edge. The shadows come in the next step.
block-in-frame.leave: Leave the sky and leaves showing inside the panes, and the blue wall beside the wide post.
block-in-frame.stop: Stop when the frame reaches the left and top edges as clean white pieces, about 4 1/4 in wide in all.

shade-frame.first: Let the white frame dry, or the lavender will turn chalky as it mixes in.
shade-frame.start: Start on the inner face of the wide post, where it turns away from the light, pulling down from the top edge.
shade-frame.strokes: Lay each strip as a narrow straight piece along its piece of frame: down the uprights, under the crossbar, along the lower face of the bottom ledge.
shade-frame.inside: The lavender sits only on the faces turned away from the window light, so the frame looks deep; its middle is about 2 in from the left edge.
shade-frame.leave: Leave the white lit faces of the frame clean beside each strip, and the panes untouched.
shade-frame.stop: Stop when every piece of the frame has a thin lavender shadow face next to its white face.

lay-in-sill.first: Let the wall and the frame dry, so the brown doesn't drag blue into it along the join.
lay-in-sill.start: Start along the join with the wall, about 6 1/4 in from the top edge, and work down toward the bottom edge.
lay-in-sill.strokes: Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right, all the way across the canvas.
lay-in-sill.inside: The whole ledge is one flat warm brown, running straight through where the blanket will lie.
lay-in-sill.leave: Leave the blue wall and the white frame clean above the ledge's back edge.
lay-in-sill.stop: Stop when the ledge reaches the left, right and bottom edges and no white canvas shows anywhere.

darken-sill-front.first: Let the flat brown ledge dry first.
darken-sill-front.start: Start along the back of the ledge where it meets the wall, about 6 1/2 in from the top edge.
darken-sill-front.strokes: Pull long level streaks across, left and right, letting them break up as the brush runs out of paint.
darken-sill-front.inside: The streaks crowd along the back of the ledge as wood grain, and a thinner dark band runs along the front face at the bottom edge.
darken-sill-front.leave: Leave plenty of the flat brown from step 7 showing between the streaks, most of all at the left end of the sill.
darken-sill-front.stop: Stop when the ledge reads as streaky wood across its whole width. Don't fill it solid: the gaps make the grain.

sunlit-sill.first: Let the dark streaks from step 8 dry, or the dry brush will smear them.
sunlit-sill.start: Start at the left end of the sill, where the window light lands; the light patch's middle is about 4 1/2 in from the left edge.
sunlit-sill.strokes: Dip only the tip, wipe it, and skim lightly in slanting bars that run from the window across the ledge.
sunlit-sill.inside: The light bars sit at the left end of the sill, nearest the window, with the frame's shadows breaking them into bars.
sunlit-sill.leave: Leave brown showing between the bars and all along the rest of the ledge.
sunlit-sill.stop: Stop when broken peach bars reach the left edge and bottom edge. If it went solid, let it dry and dry-brush brown back over part of it.

block-in-blanket.start: Start with a long rounded rectangle lying along the sill; its top is about 6 in from the top edge.
block-in-blanket.strokes: Build it in pieces: the long middle first, then curved pieces at each end like ( ), so the ends come out round.
block-in-blanket.inside: The whole blanket is one flat golden yellow, painted straight through where the cat will lie.
block-in-blanket.leave: Leave a strip of the sill showing along the bottom edge and at the left end of the sill, and the wall above.
block-in-blanket.stop: Stop when the shape runs to the right edge, about 14 3/4 in wide and 5 in tall, flat and smooth.

shade-blanket.first: Let the flat yellow blanket dry first.
shade-blanket.start: Start under the rolled top edge at the left end, where the roll curls toward the window.
shade-blanket.strokes: Bend every stroke with the roll: start at the top of each bump and pull down and around its curve, like wrapping a tube.
shade-blanket.inside: The shadow goes under the rolled top, along the fold, along the base where it meets the sill, and in the hollow where the cat will lie, because the light comes from the upper left.
shade-blanket.leave: Leave the golden yellow showing on the tops of the rolls, where the light hits.
shade-blanket.stop: Stop when the blanket looks thick and rolled, reaching the right edge.

dark-knit-loops.first: Let the shadows from step 11 dry, so the loops stay crisp.
dark-knit-loops.start: Start along the rolled top edge, pressing the first marks in a row along the roll.
dark-knit-loops.strokes: Touch the tip down, press so it spreads, then pull and lift to a point. Pair the commas into small V shapes that follow each roll's curve.
dark-knit-loops.inside: Rows of loops cover the whole blanket out to the right edge, bending with each roll and the fold.
dark-knit-loops.leave: Leave golden yellow showing between every loop, so the stitches read as separate.
dark-knit-loops.stop: Stop when rows of dark V loops cover the blanket. If you get blobs, use less paint and lift faster.

light-knit-loops.first: Let the dark loops from step 12 dry first.
light-knit-loops.start: Start on the lit top of the roll nearest the window, at the left end of the blanket.
light-knit-loops.strokes: Press and lift small commas just above the dark loops, following the same curve.
light-knit-loops.inside: Put most of them in the left half of the blanket's knit loops, on the tops of the rolls, where the window light falls.
light-knit-loops.leave: Leave the dark loops from step 12 showing under and beside every light one, and fewer light loops than dark.
light-knit-loops.stop: Stop when the rolls look chunky and knitted, with the light marks fading out toward the right edge.

block-in-cat.first: Let the blanket dry completely, so the gray doesn't pick up yellow.
block-in-cat.start: Start with a big oval for the curled body on the blanket; its middle is about 9 in from the left edge.
block-in-cat.strokes: Build in pieces: the oval body, a circle for the head at the left end of the body, two triangle ears, then curved pieces to round the edges.
block-in-cat.inside: The whole cat is one flat gray. The head overlaps the window frame, and the top of one ear sits about 1 1/2 in from the top edge.
block-in-cat.leave: Leave a band of the knit loops showing below the cat.
block-in-cat.stop: Stop when the cat's shape reaches the right edge, about 14 3/4 in wide and 7 in tall, with no shading.

shade-cat.first: Let the flat gray cat dry first.
shade-cat.start: Start along the far end of the back, where the body curves down toward the blanket.
shade-cat.strokes: Bend each stroke around the body: from the top of the back down along its curve, and around the head and the ears.
shade-cat.inside: The dark goes on the far end of the back, where the body meets the blanket, along the ear edges, and in the curved hollow between head and body, away from the window light.
shade-cat.leave: Leave the flat gray showing on the top of the back, the face and the patch where the paws will go.
shade-cat.stop: Stop when the cat looks round, darker away from the window and underneath.

paint-white-patches.first: Let the dark shading dry, or the white turns gray.
paint-white-patches.start: Start with the white muzzle and chin under the face; that group's middle is about 5 1/4 in from the left edge.
paint-white-patches.strokes: Bend each stroke with the shape: around the round paws, down the chin, and in short pointed strokes for the fluffy edges of the chest blaze.
paint-white-patches.inside: The white goes on the muzzle and chin, the two paws resting on the blanket, and the chest blaze, whose middle is about 9 1/4 in from the left edge.
paint-white-patches.leave: Leave gray between the two paws and all around the blaze, so each patch reads alone.
paint-white-patches.stop: Stop when the muzzle, the blaze and two plump paws are clean white.

paint-ear-insides.first: Let the gray ears dry first.
paint-ear-insides.start: Start in the ear near the window; its middle is about 2 1/4 in from the left edge.
paint-ear-insides.strokes: Touch the tip down near the ear's point, press to spread, and pull toward the ear's base, lifting off.
paint-ear-insides.inside: The pink fills the inside of both ears; the upright ear's middle is about 6 1/4 in from the left edge.
paint-ear-insides.leave: Leave a gray rim around the edge of each ear.
paint-ear-insides.stop: Stop when both ears have soft pink insides inside their gray rims.

paint-stripes.first: Let the white patches and pink ears dry first.
paint-stripes.start: Start on the top of the back, pressing the full brush down where each stripe begins.
paint-stripes.strokes: Press the full width at the spine, then turn onto the edge and lighten as you pull down the side, so each stripe tapers to a point.
paint-stripes.inside: The stripes wrap around the forehead, the cheeks, the back and side, and across the tail; most of them sit in the right half of the stripes.
paint-stripes.leave: Leave the white patches, the pink ears and gray between every stripe.
paint-stripes.stop: Stop when tapered stripes wrap the head, body and tail. Don't make them straight: they curve with the body.

flick-fur.first: Let the stripes dry, or the flicks will smear them.
flick-fur.start: Start on the head and around the face; the flicks' middle is about 8 in from the left edge.
flick-fur.strokes: Load lightly and flick quickly along the curve of the body, lifting off as you go so each mark thins at the end.
flick-fur.inside: The flicks go over the gray coat and the stripe edges, thickest on the head, the back and the chest, where the light reaches.
flick-fur.leave: Leave the stripes and the darker gray showing between the flicks.
flick-fur.stop: Stop when the coat looks soft and furry. Too much paint makes flat blobs.

line-eyes.first: Let the fur flicks dry, so the lines stay sharp instead of feathering.
line-eyes.start: Start with the closed eye nearest the window, a curved line on the face.
line-eyes.strokes: Thin the paint, hold the liner upright and pull each eye as a gentle downward curve, starting thick and lightening.
line-eyes.inside: Add a small mouth line under the muzzle and short lines between the toes on the paws.
line-eyes.leave: Leave the white muzzle and paws clean around each line.
line-eyes.stop: Stop when the cat has two sleepy curved eyes, a mouth and toes. Skippy lines mean you need more water.

press-nose.first: Let the eye and mouth lines dry first.
press-nose.start: Start on the white muzzle; the nose's left side is about 5 1/2 in from the left edge.
press-nose.strokes: Touch the tip down at the top of the nose, press to spread, and lift down to a point.
press-nose.inside: The nose is one small triangle, about 3/4 in wide, sitting just above the mouth line.
press-nose.leave: Leave the white muzzle showing all around the nose.
press-nose.stop: Stop after one clean pink triangle. Don't go over it again, or it will blob.

line-whiskers.start: Start at the muzzle; the first fan's middle is about 5 1/2 in from the left edge.
line-whiskers.strokes: Thin the paint, hold the liner upright and pull each whisker out from the muzzle, lightening as you go so it tapers.
line-whiskers.inside: One fan crosses the gray cheek and the paws; the other runs toward the chest blaze, its middle about 9 1/4 in from the left edge.
line-whiskers.leave: Leave the face, eyes and nose untouched.
line-whiskers.stop: Stop after a few fine whiskers on each side. Reload often.

Keep the paler blue close to the window, where the light falls, and the deeper blue toward the right edge and the top edge.
Leave the bottom of the canvas bare; the wall's lower edge sits about 6 in from the bottom edge and slopes down gently toward the right edge.
Stop when the wall reaches the left, right and top edges as one soft criss-cross blue, with no cat or blanket on it yet.

block-in-frame.text: Let the wall and the window view dry, so the white stays clean.
Start with the wide upright post where the window view meets the wall, pulling it down from the top edge.
Build the frame from straight pieces: the wide post, a thinner upright, a crossbar across the upper view, then the wide ledge along the bottom of the window.
The whole frame is flat white for now; its middle is about 1 3/4 in from the left edge. The shadows come in the next step.
Leave the sky and leaves showing through the window between the pieces, and keep the blue wall clean where the post meets it.
Stop when the frame reaches the left and top edges as clean white pieces, about 4 1/4 in wide in all.

shade-frame.text: Let the white frame dry, or the lavender will turn chalky as it mixes in.
Start on the inner face of the wide post, where it turns away from the light, pulling down from the top edge.
You build in straight pieces again, as in step 5, but with a smaller brush and only on the shadow faces.
Lay each strip as a narrow straight piece along its piece of frame: down the uprights, under the crossbar, along the lower face of the bottom ledge.
The lavender sits only on the faces turned away from the window light, so the frame looks deep; its middle is about 2 in from the left edge.
Leave the white lit faces of the frame clean, and the view through the window untouched.
Stop when every piece of the frame has a thin lavender shadow face as well as a white lit face.

lay-in-sill.text: Let the wall and the frame dry, so the brown doesn't drag blue into it along the join.
Start along the join with the wall, about 6 1/4 in from the top edge, and work down toward the bottom edge.
Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right, all the way across the canvas.
The whole ledge is one flat warm brown, running straight through where the blanket will lie.
Keep the blue wall and the white frame clean along the join where the ledge meets them.
Stop when the ledge reaches the left, right and bottom edges and no white canvas shows anywhere.

darken-sill-front.text: Let the flat brown ledge dry first.
Start along the back of the ledge, right where it meets the wall.
The same long level strokes as step 7, but now with a darker mix and a smaller brush, letting them break into streaks.
Pull long level streaks across, left and right, letting them break up as the brush runs out of paint.
The streaks crowd along the back of the ledge as wood grain, and a thinner dark band runs along the front face at the bottom edge.
Leave plenty of the flat brown from step 7 showing between the streaks, most of all at the left end of the sill.
Stop when the ledge reads as streaky wood across its whole width. Don't fill it solid: the gaps make the grain.

sunlit-sill.text: Let the dark streaks from step 8 dry, or the dry brush will smear them.
Start at the left end of the sill, where the window light lands on the ledge.
Dip only the tip, wipe it, and skim lightly in slanting bars that run from the window across the ledge.
The light bars sit at the left end of the sill, nearest the window, with the frame's shadows breaking them into bars.
Leave brown showing between the bars and all along the rest of the ledge.
Stop when broken peach bars reach the left edge and bottom edge. If it went solid, let it dry and dry-brush brown back over part of it.

block-in-blanket.text: Start with a long rounded rectangle lying along the sill; its top is about 6 in from the top edge.
You built the window frame from pieces in step 5; the blanket is built the same way, with round pieces instead of straight ones.
Build it in pieces: the long middle first, then curved pieces at each end like ( ), so the ends come out round.
The whole blanket is one flat golden yellow, painted straight through where the cat will lie.
Leave a strip of the sill's front showing, and the sunlit bars at the left end of the sill.
Stop when the shape runs to the right edge, about 14 3/4 in wide and 5 in tall, flat and smooth.

shade-blanket.text: Let the flat yellow blanket dry first.
Start under the rolled top edge at the left end, where the roll curls toward the window.
Bend every stroke with the roll: start at the top of each bump and pull down and around its curve, like wrapping a tube.
The shadow goes under the rolled top, along the fold, along the base where it meets the sill, and in the hollow where the cat will lie, because the light comes from the upper left.
Leave the bright flat yellow from step 10 showing on the tops of the rolls, where the light hits.
Stop when the blanket looks thick and rolled, reaching the right edge.

dark-knit-loops.text: Let the shadows from step 11 dry, so the loops stay crisp.
Start along the rolled top edge, pressing the first marks in a row along the roll.
This is the Dark gold from the shadows in step 11, now pressed into small commas with a round brush.
Touch the tip down, press so it spreads, then pull and lift to a point. Pair the commas into small V shapes that follow each roll's curve.
Rows of loops cover the whole blanket out to the right edge, bending with each roll and the fold.
Leave the bright yellow from step 10 showing between every loop, so the stitches read as separate.
Stop when rows of dark V loops cover the blanket. If you get blobs, use less paint and lift faster.

light-knit-loops.text: Let the dark loops from step 12 dry first.
Start on the lit top of the roll nearest the window, at the left end of the blanket.
The same press and lift as the dark loops in step 12, with a smaller brush and fewer marks, only where the light falls.
Press and lift small commas just above the dark loops, following the same curve.
Put most of them in the left half of the blanket's knit loops, on the tops of the rolls, where the window light falls.
Leave the dark loops from step 12 showing all through, and make fewer light loops than dark.
Stop when the rolls look chunky and knitted, with the light marks fading out toward the right edge.

block-in-cat.text: Let the blanket dry completely, so the gray doesn't pick up yellow.
Start with a big oval for the curled body on the blanket; its middle is about 9 in from the left edge.
You built the blanket from pieces in step 10; build the cat the same way, an oval body first, then the head and ears.
Build in pieces: the oval body, a circle for the head at the left end of the body, two triangle ears, then curved pieces to round the edges.
The whole cat is one flat gray.
Leave a band of the knit loops showing below the cat.
Stop when the cat's shape reaches the right edge, about 14 3/4 in wide and 7 in tall, with no shading.

shade-cat.text: Let the flat gray cat dry first.
Start along the far end of the back, where the body curves down toward the blanket.
The same curved strokes you used to round the blanket in step 11, now wrapping around the cat's body and head.
Bend each stroke around the body: from the top of the back down along its curve, and around the head and the ears.
The dark goes on the far end of the back, where the body meets the blanket, along the ear edges, and in the curved hollow between head and body, away from the window light.
Leave the flat gray showing on the top of the back, the face and the patch where the paws will go.
Stop when the cat looks round, darker away from the window and underneath.

paint-white-patches.text: Let the dark shading dry, or the white turns gray.
Start with the white muzzle and chin under the face; that group's middle is about 5 1/4 in from the left edge.
Curved strokes again, as in step 15, but with a small round brush and short strokes that follow each paw and patch.
Bend each stroke with the shape: around the round paws, down the chin, and in short pointed strokes for the fluffy edges of the chest blaze.
The white goes on the muzzle and chin, the two paws resting on the blanket, and the chest blaze, whose middle is about 9 1/4 in from the left edge.
Leave gray between the two paws and all around the blaze, so each patch reads alone.
Stop when the muzzle, the blaze and two plump paws are clean white.

paint-ear-insides.text: Let the gray ears dry first.
Start in the ear near the window; its middle is about 2 1/4 in from the left edge.
The same press and lift as the knit loops in step 12, now one or two longer strokes filling each ear.
Touch the tip down near the ear's point, press to spread, and pull toward the ear's base, lifting off.
The pink fills the inside of both ears; the upright ear's middle is about 6 1/4 in from the left edge.
Leave a gray rim around the edge of each ear.
Stop when both ears have soft pink insides with a gray rim still showing around each.

paint-stripes.text: Let the white patches and pink ears dry first.
Start on the top of the back, pressing the full brush down where each stripe begins.
Press the full width at the spine, then turn onto the edge and lighten as you pull down the side, so each stripe tapers to a point.
The stripes wrap around the forehead, the cheeks, the back and side, and across the tail; most of them sit in the right half of the stripes.
Leave the white patches, the pink ears and gray between every stripe.
Stop when tapered stripes wrap the head, body and tail. Don't make them straight: they curve with the body.

flick-fur.text: Let the stripes dry, or the flicks will smear them.
Start on the head and around the face; the flicks' middle is about 8 in from the left edge.
Load lightly and flick quickly along the curve of the body, lifting off as you go so each mark thins at the end.
The flicks go over the gray coat and the stripe edges, thickest on the head, the back and the chest, where the light reaches.
Leave the stripes and the darker gray showing between the flicks.
Stop when the coat looks soft and furry. Too much paint makes flat blobs.

line-eyes.text: Let the fur flicks dry, so the lines stay sharp instead of feathering.
Start with the closed eye nearest the window, a curved line on the face.
This is the Charcoal brown from the stripes in step 18, now thinned and pulled as fine lines with the liner.
Thin the paint, hold the liner upright and pull each eye as a gentle downward curve, starting thick and lightening.
Add a small mouth line under the muzzle and short lines between the toes on the paws.
Leave the white muzzle and paws clean around each line.
Stop when the cat has two sleepy curved eyes, a mouth and toes. Skippy lines mean you need more water.

press-nose.text: Let the eye and mouth lines dry first.
Start on the white muzzle; the nose's left side is about 5 1/2 in from the left edge.
The same Rosy pink and the same press and lift as the ears in step 17, now one tiny mark with the smallest round brush.
Touch the tip down at the top of the nose, press to spread, and lift down to a point.
The nose is one small triangle, about 3/4 in wide, sitting where the muzzle meets the small mouth line.
Leave the white muzzle showing all around the nose.
Stop after one clean pink triangle. Don't go over it again, or it will blob.

line-whiskers.text: Start at the muzzle; the first fan's middle is about 5 1/2 in from the left edge.
The same thin liner lines as the eyes in step 20, now pulled long and fine, out from the muzzle.
Thin the paint, hold the liner upright and pull each whisker out from the muzzle, lightening as you go so it tapers.
One fan crosses the gray cheek and the paws; the other runs toward the chest blaze, its middle about 9 1/4 in from the left edge.
Leave the face, eyes and nose untouched.
Stop after a few fine whiskers on each side. Reload often.

opening.welcome: You are about to paint a gray tabby kitten curled up asleep on a golden knit blanket, in a sunny window. The heart of it is the sleeping face: closed eyes, a pink nose, a white muzzle with whiskers, and two white paws tucked in close. The mood is warm and quiet, a kitten soaking up the afternoon light.
opening.light: The light comes in through the window and falls across everything in the room. Where it lands you will paint things paler and brighter, the sunny bars on the sill and the tops of the blanket's rolls. The sides that turn away from the window get the darker paint, so the cat and the blanket look round.

skills.how: You make a big shape from simple pieces: a rectangle or an oval first, then curved pieces around it. You build the window frame, the folded blanket and the curled cat this way. Start with the biggest piece, and don't worry about small gaps where pieces meet.

You touch the brush tip down, press so it spreads, then pull and lift to a point, which leaves a little comma. Rows of these become the blanket's chunky knit, and single ones make the pink ears and nose. If you get blobs, use less paint and lift faster.

You bend every stroke with the shape, starting at the crest of each bump and following its curve. It is what makes the blanket's rolls and the cat's body look round instead of flat. Keep the darker paint on the side turned away from the window light.

opening.road: We paint from the farthest thing to the nearest. First the bright view through the window, then the blue wall and the white window frame, then the wooden sill with its grain and sunny bars. Next comes the blanket, painted straight through where the cat will lie, so the cat can sit on it. Most of the lesson goes to the cat: its shape, its shadow, white patches, pink ears, stripes and fur. The face comes last, so the sleeping eyes, nose and whiskers get the freshest, sharpest marks.

the-window-view.for: This stage paints the farthest thing in the picture, the sky and leaves seen through the window.
the-window-view.end: A small patch of soft blue sky with white cloud holes and a few leaf taps sits in the corner, and the rest of the canvas is bare.

the-wall-and-frame.for: This stage paints the blue wall and the white window frame that stand in front of the view.
the-wall-and-frame.end: A soft criss-cross blue wall fills the room, with a white window frame and its lavender shadow faces, and the sill's space is still bare white.

the-windowsill.for: This stage lays the wooden sill that the blanket and cat will rest on.
the-windowsill.end: A warm brown ledge with dark grain streaks runs the width of the canvas, with peach sunny bars at the window end, and no white canvas shows.

the-blanket.for: This stage builds the folded golden blanket and gives it its chunky knit.
the-blanket.end: A thick rolled golden blanket lies on the sill, its knit loops dark in the folds and bright on the lit rolls, with no cat on it yet.

the-cat-shape.for: This stage builds the curled cat as one shape, rounds it with shadow, and adds its white patches.
the-cat-shape.end: A round gray cat lies curled on the blanket, darker away from the window, with a white muzzle, a white chest blaze and two white paws.

the-markings.for: This stage gives the cat its pink ears and its tabby stripes.
the-markings.end: The cat has pink ears with gray rims and dark tapered stripes wrapping its head, body and tail.

the-fur.for: This stage turns the smooth coat into soft fur.
the-fur.end: The coat looks furry, with light flicks over the gray and the stripes still showing through.

the-face.for: This stage brings the sleeping face to life, the focal point of the painting.
the-face.end: The kitten has closed sleepy eyes, toes, a small pink nose and fine white whiskers, and the painting is finished.

back.text: The same dry tap you used for the far leaves in step 2, now with a paler mix and only a few taps.
You build in straight pieces again, as in step 5, but with a smaller brush and only on the shadow faces.
The same long level strokes as step 7, but now with a darker mix and a smaller brush, letting them break into streaks.
You built the window frame from pieces in step 5; the blanket is built the same way, with round pieces instead of straight ones.
This is the Dark gold from the shadows in step 11, now pressed into small commas with a round brush.
The same press and lift as the dark loops in step 12, with a smaller brush and fewer marks, only where the light falls.
You built the blanket from pieces in step 10; build the cat the same way, an oval body first, then the head and ears.
The same curved strokes you used to round the blanket in step 11, now wrapping around the cat's body and head.
Curved strokes again, as in step 15, but with a small round brush and short strokes that follow each paw and patch.
The same press and lift as the knit loops in step 12, now one or two longer strokes filling each ear.
This is the Charcoal brown from the stripes in step 18, now thinned and pulled as fine lines with the liner.
The same Rosy pink and the same press and lift as the ears in step 17, now one tiny mark with the smallest round brush.
The same thin liner lines as the eyes in step 20, now pulled long and fine, out from the muzzle.

taken_out.sentence: The head overlaps the window frame, and the top of the sleeping tabby cat is about 1 1/2 in from the top edge.
taken_out.why: step 14 (block-in-cat), line 4 (inside): "about 1 1/2 in from the top edge" says 1 1/2 in from the top edge; sheet: The white window frame, its top: nearest from the top edge 0 in

blend-sky.start: Start in the upper left corner of the canvas with Soft blue-gray. Work across and down in rows until the whole canvas is covered, edge to edge.
blend-sky.strokes: Make short X strokes that cross each other with the 1 inch flat. While the blue is still wet, cross Golden orange and a little Pale yellow into it so the colors melt together.
blend-sky.inside: Keep blue as the main color everywhere. Put the gold in loose slanting streaks across the middle and toward the top, where the sun's glow will spread later.
blend-sky.leave: No white canvas should show anywhere. Let the X marks stay visible as a soft texture.
blend-sky.stop: Stop when the canvas is a soft blue sky with warm gold streaks drifting through it and no hard edges. Let it dry completely.

paint-sun.first: The sky from step 1 must be dry.
paint-sun.start: Put the sun high in the sky, its middle about 10 1/2 in from the left edge and 2 in from the top edge.
paint-sun.strokes: Circle Sun cream round and round with the tip of the #10 round to make the small disk. Then circle Pale yellow outward from it, each ring wider and softer.
paint-sun.inside: The disk stays creamy and brightest in its middle. The yellow glow spreads around it about a hand's width and reaches up to the top edge.
paint-sun.leave: Leave the blue and gold sky from step 1 showing everywhere beyond the glow.
paint-sun.stop: A soft glowing sun whose bumpy edge melts into the sky. If the glow ends in a hard ring, soften it with lighter circles.

pull-far-trunks.first: The sun from step 2 must be dry.
pull-far-trunks.start: Start at the top edge, right of the low sun, with the tallest trunk. The middle of this step's paint is about 14 1/4 in from the left edge.
pull-far-trunks.strokes: Press the full width of the 1/2 inch flat and pull each trunk straight down toward the bottom edge. Turn onto the brush's edge and lighten the pressure for the thin stubby branches.
pull-far-trunks.inside: Paint two tall trunks from the top edge down to the bottom edge, with a few shorter, fainter trunks and stubby branches between them. Keep them soft and plain, with no bark, because they are far away.
pull-far-trunks.leave: Leave the sun's glow and the rest of the sky untouched.
pull-far-trunks.stop: Two tall hazy blue trunks and their fainter neighbors stand near the right edge of the canvas, soft-edged, with sky between them.

dab-dark-far-leaves.first: The trunks from step 3 must be dry.
dab-dark-far-leaves.start: Begin with the patch in the upper middle of the canvas. Its top is about 2 3/4 in from the top edge, and its middle is about 5 in from the left edge.
dab-dark-far-leaves.strokes: Tap Red-orange with the tip of the old stiff brush, wiped almost dry. Tap more in the middle of each patch so it gets solid, and fewer at its ragged edge.
dab-dark-far-leaves.inside: Make loose clumps: one in the upper middle, clumps around the hazy far trunks up near the top edge, small bits at the left edge, and two clumps near the bottom edge.
dab-dark-far-leaves.leave: Leave plenty of blue and gold sky between the clumps, and let the far trunks show through the clumps around them.
dab-dark-far-leaves.stop: Scattered soft red-orange clumps that look like distant treetops. If you get blobs instead of dabs, wipe the brush on a paper towel and tap again.

dab-light-far-leaves.first: The red-orange dabs from step 4 must be dry.
dab-light-far-leaves.start: Start around the sun's glow and work outward and down through the middle of the canvas. The middle of this step's paint is about 8 1/4 in from the left edge.
dab-light-far-leaves.strokes: Tap Light orange with the tip of the dry old stiff brush. Build loose clumps that join into one big hazy mass.
dab-light-far-leaves.inside: Spread it widely: around the sun, over the middle, and down toward the bottom, plus touches on the clumps at the left edge and around the far trunks. Put the most on the sides of the red-orange clumps that face the sun.
dab-light-far-leaves.leave: Leave some of the red-orange from step 4 showing underneath. Keep the far trunks visible and blue sky around the mass.
dab-light-far-leaves.stop: A big soft orange glow of hazy autumn woods fills the middle of the canvas, with darker clumps and blue sky around it.

block-in-branch.first: The orange dabs from step 5 must be dry.
block-in-branch.start: Start with the trunk: one long band from the bottom edge up near the left edge, all the way to the top edge.
block-in-branch.strokes: Build it in pieces with the 1/2 inch flat. Lay the trunk band first, then the branch in curved pieces, leaving the trunk low down and arching up across the canvas and down again.
block-in-branch.inside: The branch is thick where it leaves the trunk and thins to a point at its far end. The right side of that point is about 2 1/2 in from the right edge. Fill everything with flat Bark brown.
block-in-branch.leave: Leave the background showing all around the wood, with no gaps of sky inside the brown.
block-in-branch.stop: A flat brown trunk and one big arching branch, solid and even, with no shading yet.

block-in-leaves.first: The brown branch from step 6 must be dry.
block-in-leaves.start: Start with the gold leaf at the top edge, near the trunk. Its middle is about 4 in from the left edge.
block-in-leaves.strokes: With the #8 round, lay a center teardrop for each leaf. Then add pointed curved pieces on each side, smaller toward the tip, to give each leaf a jagged edge.
block-in-leaves.inside: Paint four leaves. The first is Golden yellow at the top edge, with a Red-orange leaf just under it. The other two hang from the branch: a Golden yellow leaf whose top is about 8 in from the top edge, then a Red-orange leaf further along.
block-in-leaves.leave: Leave the branch and the background around each leaf untouched.
block-in-leaves.stop: Four flat, solid leaf shapes, two gold and two red-orange, with no veins or shading yet.

shade-leaves.first: The leaves from step 7 must be dry.
shade-leaves.start: Start on the gold leaf at the top edge, down its center from the end where the stem will join.
shade-leaves.strokes: Dip only the tip of the 1/4 inch flat and wipe it nearly dry. Skim Deep gold along each gold leaf and Deep red along each red leaf, from the stem end toward the tip.
shade-leaves.inside: Darken the center and the stem end of each leaf, which are turned away from the sun. On the red leaves it covers the half nearest the stem. Add two tiny touches on the brown wood from step 6.
shade-leaves.leave: Leave each leaf's own bright color showing toward its tip and outer edges.
shade-leaves.stop: Each leaf has a broken darker half and a brighter half, so it looks curved. If it went on solid, let it dry and dry-brush the leaf color back over part of it.

light-leaves.first: The shading from step 8 must be dry.
light-leaves.start: Start on the upper red leaf, on the half toward its tip.
light-leaves.strokes: Dry-brush with the tip of the 1/4 inch flat, skimming lightly from the shaded part toward the leaf's tip. Use Coral orange on the red leaves and Golden yellow on the gold ones.
light-leaves.inside: Brighten the tip halves of the red leaves and the middles of the gold leaves, where they face the sun. Add a few tiny warm flecks along the trunk and the branch.
light-leaves.leave: Leave the darker shading from step 8 showing near each stem, and keep the leaves' edges ragged.
light-leaves.stop: Each leaf now runs from dark to bright and looks lit, with a few warm specks on the wood. Keep the strokes broken, never solid.

shade-branch.first: The leaves and flecks from step 9 must be dry.
shade-branch.start: Start at the bottom edge, where the trunk and branch join, and work up the trunk toward the top edge.
shade-branch.strokes: Skim the nearly dry 1/2 inch flat along the wood in short broken strokes: lengthwise up the trunk, then along the branch's curve out to its point.
shade-branch.inside: Darken the underside of the branch and most of the trunk, the parts turned away from the sun, in broken patches like rough bark.
shade-branch.leave: Leave a band of plain mid brown along the arch of the branch where the sun hits it. Keep the leaves clean.
shade-branch.stop: The wood looks rough and round: dark broken bark underneath, mid brown along its sunny arch. If it goes on solid, use less paint and skim more lightly.

light-branch.first: The dark bark from step 10 must be dry.
light-branch.start: Start up the trunk's sunny edge. The middle of the trunk's light is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge.
light-branch.strokes: Skim the nearly dry 1/4 inch flat in long broken strokes along the wood: up the trunk, then along the arch of the branch out toward its point.
light-branch.inside: Keep the light to a thin rim where the sun hits: the edge of the trunk that faces the sun, and the arch of the branch. Make it brightest along the stretch where the bird will sit.
light-branch.leave: Leave the mid brown and the dark bark from step 10 showing. The light is only a rim.
light-branch.stop: A thin, broken warm rim of light runs along the wood and makes it look round and sunlit.

line-twigs-stems-veins.first: Everything from step 11 must be dry, because liner lines spread on wet paint.
line-twigs-stems-veins.start: Start at the far point of the branch and pull twigs out to the right edge of the canvas.
line-twigs-stems-veins.strokes: Thin the paint with water and hold the liner upright. Pull each line with light pressure, thick where it leaves the wood and tapering to a point. Let the twigs fork.
line-twigs-stems-veins.inside: Add three twigs forking from the branch's end and a stem from each hanging leaf up to the wood. Add a thin twig from the trunk to the top leaves, and a center vein with a few side veins in each leaf.
line-twigs-stems-veins.leave: Leave the leaf colors and the lit wood showing. Keep the veins thin.
line-twigs-stems-veins.stop: Twigs reach the edge, and every leaf hangs on a stem and has veins. If the lines skip, the paint is too thick: add water.

block-in-chickadee.first: The twigs and veins from step 12 must be dry.
block-in-chickadee.start: Start with a big oval body sitting on the arch of the branch. The middle of the bird is about 6 3/4 in from the left edge.
block-in-chickadee.strokes: Build the bird from pieces with the 1/2 inch flat. Lay the oval body first, then a round head on top whose top is about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, then the tapering tail.
block-in-chickadee.inside: Fill the whole bird with flat Warm buff. The tail slants down toward the trunk until it almost touches the branch.
block-in-chickadee.leave: Leave the branch showing where the belly rests on it. The bird sits on the branch, not over it.
block-in-chickadee.stop: One smooth, flat buff bird shape: round body, round head, long tail. Give it a second coat if the background shows through.

shade-chickadee.first: The buff bird from step 13 must be dry.
shade-chickadee.start: Start where the belly rests on the branch.
shade-chickadee.strokes: Pull curved strokes with the 1/2 inch flat that wrap around the round body. Run them down the tail and over the head, following each shape.
shade-chickadee.inside: Cover most of the bird thinly, and press more paint where the belly rests on the branch, the part turned away from the sun.
shade-chickadee.leave: Leave the plain buff from step 13 on the face and on the sunny front of the chest.
shade-chickadee.stop: The bird looks round: darker at the belly, lighter toward the sun, with curved stroke marks showing.

paint-white-patches.first: The shading from step 14 must be dry.
paint-white-patches.start: Start on the face, across the head where the cheek goes. The middle of this step's paint is about 8 in from the left edge.
paint-white-patches.strokes: With the #8 round, curve each stroke around the head, following its roundness. Put it on in 2 to 3 thin coats.
paint-white-patches.inside: Paint a wide creamy band across the head, from the front of the face back toward the neck, fading to golden where it meets the chest.
paint-white-patches.leave: Leave the crown and the throat buff for now, because the cap and bib go there.
paint-white-patches.stop: A clean creamy band across the head, soft where it meets the body. Several thin coats, dried in between, look better than one thick coat.

paint-cap-bib.first: The white cheek from step 15 must be dry.
paint-cap-bib.start: Start with the cap over the crown. Its middle is about 7 1/4 in from the left edge, and its top is about 1 1/2 in from the top edge.
paint-cap-bib.strokes: With the #6 round, curve strokes over the round crown, then curve the bib under the face and down the throat. On the wing and tail, pull long curved strokes down and back toward the tail tip.
paint-cap-bib.inside: The black goes on the cap, the bib, and loose streaks along the wing and down the tail.
paint-cap-bib.leave: Leave the white cheek as a clean band between the cap and the bib, and let the buff body show between the wing streaks.
paint-cap-bib.stop: A bold black cap and bib frame the white cheek, and broken dark streaks mark the wing and tail.

paint-wing-tail.first: The black from step 16 must be dry.
paint-wing-tail.start: Start at the back of the neck, just behind the black cap.
paint-wing-tail.strokes: With the 1/4 inch flat, lay short curved strokes that follow the feathers down and back toward the tail.
paint-wing-tail.inside: Add only small touches: a couple behind the cap and at the back of the neck, a few along the dark wing streaks, and a little near the tail tip.
paint-wing-tail.leave: Leave the dark streaks from step 16 and the cap, bib and cheek showing. These are small touches, not a full coat.
paint-wing-tail.stop: A few cool gray touches start to turn the streaked wing into feathers.

line-wing-feathers.first: The gray touches from step 17 must be dry.
line-wing-feathers.start: Start at the shoulder of the wing, where it leaves the back of the neck.
line-wing-feathers.strokes: Press the full width of the 1/4 inch angle and pull each feather line down and back along the wing, lifting so it tapers. Lay the tail as long strokes that end in points.
line-wing-feathers.inside: Fill the whole wing and tail with these overlapping feather strokes. Cover the dark streaks from step 16 so the wing reads as one slate-gray shape along the back.
line-wing-feathers.leave: Leave the cap, cheek, bib and buff body clean.
line-wing-feathers.stop: A smooth dark gray wing and a pointed tail, made of tapered feather lines. If the lines don't taper, lighten the pressure sooner.

flick-belly-feathers.first: The wing from step 18 must be dry.
flick-belly-feathers.start: Start low on the belly, just where it tucks under the wing.
flick-belly-feathers.strokes: Load the small fan lightly, touch down at the base and flick quickly, lifting off so each mark tapers. Angle the flicks down and back, like feathers lying away from the head.
flick-belly-feathers.inside: Put most of the flicks where the belly tucks under the wing, the part away from the sun, and scatter a few across the middle of the belly.
flick-belly-feathers.leave: Leave the lighter buff from earlier steps showing between the flicks, and keep off the wing.
flick-belly-feathers.stop: The belly looks soft and feathery, warmer and darker where it tucks under the wing.

flick-wing-feathers.first: The belly flicks from step 19 must be dry.
flick-wing-feathers.start: Start on the wing, at the edges of the feathers near the shoulder.
flick-wing-feathers.strokes: Load the small fan lightly and flick along each feather and down the tail, lifting off so the marks taper toward the tips.
flick-wing-feathers.inside: Separate the wing and tail feathers with fine flicks. Run a soft feathery line where the cap meets the cheek and around the bib, so the markings look feathered.
flick-wing-feathers.leave: Leave the gray and the earlier feather lines showing between the flicks.
flick-wing-feathers.stop: The wing and tail show separate feathers, and the black markings have soft, feathered edges.

flick-lit-chest.first: The flicks from step 20 must be dry.
flick-lit-chest.start: Start on the front of the chest, just past the bib, on the edge facing the sun. The middle of this step's paint is about 8 in from the left edge.
flick-lit-chest.strokes: Load the small fan lightly and flick down the chest, lifting off so each mark tapers and follows the round curve of the breast.

flick-lit-chest.leave: Leave the buff belly from step 19 showing between the flicks.
flick-lit-chest.stop: The chest glows creamy white where the sun catches it and fades into buff.

paint-eye-beak.first: The feathers from step 21 must be dry.
paint-eye-beak.start: Start with the eye, at the edge of the cap where it meets the white cheek.
paint-eye-beak.strokes: With the #2 round, touch down, press and lift. Make a small round press for the eye, a short pull ending on the tip for the beak, and a comma shape for each toe.
paint-eye-beak.inside: Add the beak at the front of the face, and two short legs with curled toes gripping the branch where the belly rests. Add a few dots near the tail tip and small dark beads along the twigs.

line-legs-feet.first: The eye and feet from step 22 must be dry.
line-legs-feet.start: Start on the legs, where they leave the belly.

dot-eye-shine.first: The legs from step 23 must be dry.
dot-eye-shine.start: Start with the eye: one tiny dot on the side of the eye facing the sun.

blend-sky.text: Start in the upper left corner of the canvas with Soft blue-gray. Work across and down in rows until the whole canvas is covered, edge to edge.

Keep blue as the main color everywhere. Put the gold in loose slanting streaks across the middle and toward the top, where the sun's glow will spread later.
No white canvas should show anywhere. Let the X marks stay visible as a soft texture.
Stop when the canvas is a soft blue sky with warm gold streaks drifting through it and no hard edges. Let it dry completely.

paint-sun.text: The sky from step 1 must be dry.
Put the sun high in the sky, its middle about 10 1/2 in from the left edge and 2 in from the top edge.
Circle Sun cream round and round with the tip of the #10 round to make the small disk. Then circle Pale yellow outward from it, each ring wider and softer.

Leave the blue and gold sky from step 1 showing everywhere beyond the glow.
A soft glowing sun whose bumpy edge melts into the sky. If the glow ends in a hard ring, soften it with lighter circles.

pull-far-trunks.text: The sun from step 2 must be dry.
Start at the top edge, right of the low sun, with the tallest trunk. The middle of this step's paint is about 14 1/4 in from the left edge.
Press the full width of the 1/2 inch flat and pull each trunk straight down toward the bottom edge. Turn onto the brush's edge and lighten the pressure for the thin stubby branches.

Paint two tall trunks from the top edge down to the bottom edge, with a few shorter, fainter trunks and stubby branches between them. Keep them soft and plain, with no bark, because they are far away.
Leave the sun's glow and the rest of the sky untouched.
Two tall hazy blue trunks and their fainter neighbors stand near the right edge of the canvas, soft-edged, with sky between them.

dab-dark-far-leaves.text: The trunks from step 3 must be dry.
Begin with the patch in the upper middle of the canvas. Its top is about 2 3/4 in from the top edge, and its middle is about 5 in from the left edge.
Tap Red-orange with the tip of the old stiff brush, wiped almost dry. Tap more in the middle of each patch so it gets solid, and fewer at its ragged edge.
Make loose clumps: one in the upper middle, clumps around the hazy far trunks up near the top edge, small bits at the left edge, and two clumps near the bottom edge.
Leave plenty of blue and gold sky between the clumps, and let the far trunks show through the clumps around them.
Scattered soft red-orange clumps that look like distant treetops. If you get blobs instead of dabs, wipe the brush on a paper towel and tap again.

dab-light-far-leaves.text: The darker dabs from step 4 must be dry.

Tap Light orange with the tip of the dry old stiff brush. Build loose clumps that join into one big hazy mass.

Spread it widely: around the sun, over the middle, and down toward the bottom, plus touches on the clumps at the left edge and around the far trunks. Put the most on the sides of the darker clumps from step 4 that face the sun.
Leave some of the darker dabs from step 4 showing underneath. Keep the far trunks visible and blue sky around the mass.
A big soft orange glow of hazy autumn woods fills the middle of the canvas, with darker clumps and blue sky around it.

block-in-branch.text: The orange dabs from step 5 must be dry.
Start with the trunk: one long band from the bottom edge up near the left edge, all the way to the top edge.
Build it in pieces with the 1/2 inch flat. Lay the trunk band first, then the branch in curved pieces, leaving the trunk low down and arching up across the canvas and down again.
The branch is thick where it leaves the trunk and thins to a point at its far end. The right side of that point is about 2 1/2 in from the right edge. Fill everything with flat Bark brown.
Leave the background showing all around the wood. Fill the wood solidly, with no gaps where the sky peeks through.
A flat brown trunk and one big arching branch, solid and even, with no shading yet.

Start with the gold leaf at the top edge, near the trunk. Its middle is about 4 in from the left edge.
With the #8 round, lay a center teardrop for each leaf. Then add pointed curved pieces on each side, smaller toward the tip, to give each leaf a jagged edge.

Paint four leaves. The first is Golden yellow at the top edge, with a Red-orange leaf just under it. The other two hang from the branch: a Golden yellow leaf whose top is about 8 in from the top edge, then a Red-orange leaf further along.
Leave the branch and the background around each leaf untouched.
Four flat, solid leaf shapes, two gold and two red-orange, with no veins or shading yet.

shade-leaves.text: The leaves from step 7 must be dry.
Start on the gold leaf at the top edge, down its center from the end where the stem will join.
Dip only the tip of the 1/4 inch flat and wipe it nearly dry. Skim Deep gold along each gold leaf and Deep red along each red leaf, from the stem end toward the tip.
Darken the center and the stem end of each leaf, which are turned away from the sun. On the red leaves it covers the half nearest the stem. Add two tiny touches on the brown wood from step 6.
Leave each leaf's own bright color showing toward its tip and outer edges.
Each leaf has a broken darker half and a brighter half, so it looks curved. If it went on solid, let it dry and dry-brush the leaf color back over part of it.

light-leaves.text: The shading from step 8 must be dry.
Start on the upper red leaf, on the half toward its tip.
Dry-brush with the tip of the 1/4 inch flat, skimming lightly from the shaded part toward the leaf's tip. Use Coral orange on the red leaves and Golden yellow on the gold ones.
Brighten the tip halves of the red leaves and the middles of the gold leaves, where they face the sun. Add a few tiny warm flecks along the trunk and the branch.
Leave the darker shading from step 8 showing near each stem, and keep the leaves' edges ragged.
Each leaf now runs from dark to bright and looks lit, with a few warm specks on the wood. Keep the strokes broken, never solid.

Start at the bottom edge, where the trunk and branch join, and work up the trunk toward the top edge.
Skim the nearly dry 1/2 inch flat along the wood in short broken strokes: lengthwise up the trunk, then along the branch's curve out to its point.
Darken the underside of the branch and most of the trunk, the parts turned away from the sun, in broken patches like rough bark.
Leave a band of plain mid brown along the arch of the branch where the sun hits it. Keep the leaves clean.
The wood looks rough and round: dark broken bark underneath, mid brown along its sunny arch. If it goes on solid, use less paint and skim more lightly.

Skim the nearly dry 1/4 inch flat in long broken strokes along the wood: up the trunk, then along the arch of the branch out toward its point.
Keep the light to a thin rim where the sun hits: the edge of the trunk that faces the sun, and the arch of the branch. Make it brightest along the stretch where the bird will sit.

Paint four leaves. The first is Golden yellow at the top edge, with a Red-orange leaf just under it. The other two hang from the branch: a Golden yellow leaf whose top is about 8 in from the top edge, then a Red-orange leaf further along.
Leave the branch and the background around each leaf untouched.
Four flat, solid leaf shapes, two gold and two red-orange, with no veins or shading yet.

shade-leaves.text: The leaves from step 7 must be dry.
Start on the gold leaf at the top edge, down its center from the end where the stem will join.
Dip only the tip of the 1/4 inch flat and wipe it nearly dry. Skim Deep gold along each gold leaf and Deep red along each red leaf, from the stem end toward the tip.
Darken the center and the stem end of each leaf, which are turned away from the sun. On the red leaves it covers the half nearest the stem. Add two tiny touches on the brown wood from step 6.
Leave each leaf's own bright color showing toward its tip and outer edges.
Each leaf has a broken darker half and a brighter half, so it looks curved. If it went on solid, let it dry and dry-brush the leaf color back over part of it.

light-leaves.text: The shading from step 8 must be dry.
Start on the upper red leaf, on the half toward its tip.
Use the same dry brush and the same skimming touch as when you shaded the leaves in step 8. This time the paint goes on the parts facing the sun.
Dry-brush with the tip of the 1/4 inch flat, skimming lightly from the shaded part toward the leaf's tip. Use Coral orange on the red leaves and Golden yellow on the gold ones.
Brighten the tip halves of the red leaves and the middles of the gold leaves, where they face the sun. Add a few tiny warm flecks along the trunk and the branch.
Leave the darker shading from step 8 showing near each stem, and keep the leaves' edges ragged.
Each leaf now runs from dark to bright and looks lit, with a few warm specks on the wood. Keep the strokes broken, never solid.

shade-branch.text: The leaves and flecks from step 9 must be dry.
Start at the bottom edge, where the trunk and branch join, and work up the trunk toward the top edge.
This is the dry brush you used to shade the leaves in step 8, now with the bigger 1/2 inch flat and long strokes along the wood.
Skim the nearly dry 1/2 inch flat along the wood in short broken strokes: lengthwise up the trunk, then along the branch's curve out to its point.
Darken the underside of the branch and most of the trunk, the parts turned away from the sun, in broken patches like rough bark.
Leave a band of plain mid brown along the arch of the branch where the sun hits it. Keep the leaves clean.
The wood looks rough and round: dark broken bark underneath, mid brown along its sunny arch. If it goes on solid, use less paint and skim more lightly.

light-branch.text: The dark bark from step 10 must be dry.
Start up the trunk's sunny edge. The middle of the trunk's light is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge.
Skim the nearly dry 1/4 inch flat in long broken strokes along the wood: up the trunk, then along the arch of the branch out toward its point.
Keep the light to a thin rim where the sun hits: the edge of the trunk that faces the sun, and the arch of the branch. Make it brightest along the stretch where the bird will sit.
Leave the mid brown and the dark bark from step 10 showing. The light is only a rim.
A thin, broken warm rim of light runs along the wood and makes it look round and sunlit.

line-twigs-stems-veins.text: Everything from step 11 must be dry, because liner lines spread on wet paint.
Start at the far point of the branch and pull twigs out to the right edge of the canvas.
This is the same Dark brown you used for the bark shadows in step 10. Now thin it with water so it flows off the liner in fine lines.
Thin the paint with water and hold the liner upright. Pull each line with light pressure, thick where it leaves the wood and tapering to a point. Let the twigs fork.
Add three twigs forking from the branch's end and a stem from each hanging leaf up to the wood. Add a thin twig from the trunk to the top leaves, and a center vein with a few side veins in each leaf.
Leave the leaf colors and the lit wood showing. Keep the veins thin.
Twigs reach the edge, and every leaf hangs on a stem and has veins. If the lines skip, the paint is too thick: add water.

block-in-chickadee.text: The twigs and veins from step 12 must be dry.
Start with a big oval body sitting on the arch of the branch. The middle of the bird is about 6 3/4 in from the left edge.
Build the bird the way you built the branch in step 6: one simple shape first, the oval body, then add the head and tail as pieces.
Build the bird from pieces with the 1/2 inch flat. Lay the oval body first, then a round head on top whose top is about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, then the tapering tail.
Fill the whole bird with flat Warm buff. The tail slants down toward the trunk until it almost touches the branch.
Leave the branch showing where the belly rests on it. The bird sits on the branch, not over it.
One smooth, flat buff bird shape: round body, round head, long tail. Give it a second coat if the background shows through.

shade-chickadee.text: The buff bird from step 13 must be dry.
Start where the belly rests on the branch.
Pull curved strokes with the 1/2 inch flat that wrap around the round body. Run them down the tail and over the head, following each shape.
Cover most of the bird thinly, and press more paint where the belly rests on the branch, the part turned away from the sun.
Leave the plain buff from step 13 on the face and on the sunny front of the chest.
The bird looks round: darker at the belly, lighter toward the sun, with curved stroke marks showing.

paint-white-patches.text: The shading from step 14 must be dry.
Start on the face, across the head where the cheek goes. The middle of this step's paint is about 8 in from the left edge.
With the #8 round, curve each stroke around the head, following its roundness. Put it on in 2 to 3 thin coats.
Paint a wide creamy band across the head, from the front of the face back toward the neck, fading to golden where it meets the chest.
Leave the crown and the throat buff for now, because the cap and bib go there.
A clean creamy band across the head, soft where it meets the body. Several thin coats, dried in between, look better than one thick coat.

paint-cap-bib.text: The white cheek from step 15 must be dry.
Start with the cap over the crown. Its middle is about 7 1/4 in from the left edge, and its top is about 1 1/2 in from the top edge.
Use the same curved strokes that followed the round head when you painted the cheek in step 15, now in black with the smaller #6 round.
With the #6 round, curve strokes over the round crown, then curve the bib under the face and down the throat. On the wing and tail, pull long curved strokes down and back toward the tail tip.
The black goes on the cap, the bib, and loose streaks along the wing and down the tail.
Leave the white cheek as a clean band between the cap and the bib, and let the buff body show between the wing streaks.
A bold black cap and bib frame the white cheek, and broken dark streaks mark the wing and tail.

paint-wing-tail.text: The black from step 16 must be dry.
Start at the back of the neck, just behind the black cap.
This is the same Soft blue-gray you crossed into the sky in step 1. Here it goes on in small curved touches on the bird.
With the 1/4 inch flat, lay short curved strokes that follow the feathers down and back toward the tail.
Add only small touches: a couple behind the cap and at the back of the neck, a few along the dark wing streaks, and a little near the tail tip.
Leave the dark streaks from step 16 and the cap, bib and cheek showing. These are small touches, not a full coat.
A few cool gray touches start to turn the streaked wing into feathers.

line-wing-feathers.text: The gray touches from step 17 must be dry.
Start at the shoulder of the wing, where it leaves the back of the neck.
This is the same press-then-lift stroke you used to pull the far trunks in step 3. Now use the angle brush, so each feather line tapers to a point.
Press the full width of the 1/4 inch angle and pull each feather line down and back along the wing, lifting so it tapers. Lay the tail as long strokes that end in points.
Fill the whole wing and tail with these overlapping feather strokes. Cover the dark streaks from step 16 so the wing reads as one slate-gray shape along the back.
Leave the cap, cheek, bib and buff body clean.
A smooth dark gray wing and a pointed tail, made of tapered feather lines. If the lines don't taper, lighten the pressure sooner.

flick-belly-feathers.text: The wing from step 18 must be dry.
Start low on the belly, just where it tucks under the wing.
This is the same Golden buff you shaded the belly with in step 14. Now it goes on as quick flicks with the small fan instead of curved strokes.
Load the small fan lightly, touch down at the base and flick quickly, lifting off so each mark tapers. Angle the flicks down and back, like feathers lying away from the head.
Put most of the flicks where the belly tucks under the wing, the part away from the sun, and scatter a few across the middle of the belly.
Leave the lighter buff from earlier steps showing between the flicks, and keep off the wing.
The belly looks soft and feathery, warmer and darker where it tucks under the wing.

flick-wing-feathers.text: The belly flicks from step 19 must be dry.
Start on the wing, at the edges of the feathers near the shoulder.
Load the small fan lightly and flick along each feather and down the tail, lifting off so the marks taper toward the tips.
Separate the wing and tail feathers with fine flicks. Run a soft feathery line where the cap meets the cheek and around the bib, so the markings look feathered.
Leave the gray and the earlier feather lines showing between the flicks.
The wing and tail show separate feathers, and the black markings have soft, feathered edges.

flick-lit-chest.text: The flicks from step 20 must be dry.
Start on the front of the chest, just past the bib, on the edge facing the sun. The middle of this step's paint is about 8 in from the left edge.
Flick just as you did on the belly in step 19, using the creamy Warm white and putting the flicks where the sun catches the chest.
Load the small fan lightly and flick down the chest, lifting off so each mark tapers and follows the round curve of the breast.
Mass the white along the sunny front of the chest and the edge of the cheek. Use fewer flicks as you move away from the sun. Add a few light flicks on the wing and near the tail tip.
Leave the buff belly from step 19 showing between the flicks.
The chest glows creamy white where the sun catches it and fades into buff.

paint-eye-beak.text: The feathers from step 21 must be dry.
Start with the eye, at the edge of the cap where it meets the white cheek.
With the #2 round, touch down, press and lift. Make a small round press for the eye, a short pull ending on the tip for the beak, and a comma shape for each toe.
Add the beak at the front of the face, and two short legs with curled toes gripping the branch where the belly rests. Add a few dots near the tail tip and small dark beads along the twigs.
Leave the white cheek clean around the eye.
The bird has a dark eye, a sharp beak, and feet that grip. If you get a blob, use less paint and lift faster.

line-legs-feet.text: The eye and feet from step 22 must be dry.
Start on the legs, where they leave the belly.
This is the same liner you used for the twigs and veins in step 12. Thin the paint the same way and keep your touch just as light.
Thin the paint and hold the liner upright. Pull light, steady lines down each leg and around each toe, tapering at the claw.
Firm up the legs and toes on the branch. Add a few small marks on the wing and at the tail tip, and a few thin touches along the hazy far trunks.
Leave the dark feet from step 22 showing. This step only sharpens them.
Thin, crisp legs and toes grip the branch. If the lines spread, the paint underneath is still wet.

dot-eye-shine.text: The legs from step 23 must be dry.
Start with the eye: one tiny dot on the side of the eye facing the sun.
This is the same Warm white you used for the cheek in step 15. Now use just one tiny fresh dot of it.
Dip the #2 round in fresh Warm white for each dot and touch it straight down once. Don't drag it.
After the eye, add a few small light dots on the chest and on the belly near the wing, and a touch on each foot where the sun hits.
Leave most of the eye dark. The shine is only a speck.
The eye sparkles and the bird looks alive. Wipe off a bad dot while it is still wet.

opening.welcome: You are about to paint a little chickadee perched on a curved branch in autumn, with red and gold leaves hanging near it and a low sun glowing through hazy orange woods. The heart of the painting is the bird's black cap, white cheek and bright dark eye, sitting close to the sun. Everything else, from the soft background to the glowing branch, is there to make that small face shine.
opening.light: All the light in this painting comes from the low sun, glowing behind the bird. The sides of the leaves, the branch and the bird that face the sun get a warm bright edge, and the sides turned away from it fall into soft shadow. Many steps ask you to put paint where that sunlight falls or where it doesn't.

skills.how: You build each big shape from simple pieces: a band or an oval first, then curved pieces added around it. Here it makes the trunk and branch, the four hanging leaves and the whole chickadee, so you never have to draw a hard outline freehand. Fill each shape flat and solid, and don't fuss with detail yet.

Dry brush means only the tip of the brush goes in the paint, wiped nearly dry and skimmed lightly over the canvas. It shades and lights the leaves and the bark, leaving broken, see-through marks that make them look round and rough. Watch for paint going on solid: that means too much on the brush, so let it dry and skim the base color back over it.

A flick is a quick, light stroke that lifts off as it goes, so each mark tapers to a point like a feather. You use it with the small fan on the belly, the wing and the sunlit chest, turning a flat bird into a soft, feathery one. Keep the brush lightly loaded, because too much paint makes flat blobs instead of feathers.

opening.road: You start with the sky and the sun, blended wet in one go, because everything else is painted over them. Next come the far woods: hazy trunks, then dabbed autumn leaves, dark first and lighter over them, so the whole background is finished before anything sharp goes on. Then you build the branch and the hanging leaves, give them shadow and light, and line in the twigs, stems and veins. The rest of the lesson belongs to the chickadee: its shape and shading, its white cheek, its black and gray markings, and then its feathers. The face and feet come last, so the eye, the heart of the painting, gets your most careful touch.

the-sky.for: This stage lays the soft blue and gold sky over the whole canvas and circles in the glowing sun.
the-sky.end: The canvas is a soft blue sky with drifting gold streaks and a pale sun wrapped in a warm yellow glow.

the-far-woods.for: This stage paints the hazy woods far away: soft blue trunks and dabbed autumn leaves, with nothing sharp, because they are distant.
the-far-woods.end: The background is finished: hazy blue trunks stand in a big soft glow of orange and red-orange leaves around the sun.

the-branch-and-leaves.for: This stage builds the trunk, the curved branch and the four hanging leaves, then gives them shadow, sunlight and fine twigs and veins.
the-branch-and-leaves.end: A rough, sunlit branch arches across the woods, with twigs reaching out and four shaded, veined leaves hanging from it.

the-chickadee-shape.for: This stage builds the chickadee as one buff shape, shades it so it looks round, and paints its creamy white cheek.
the-chickadee-shape.end: A round buff bird sits on the branch, darker at its belly, with a creamy white band across its head.

the-markings.for: This stage gives the chickadee its black cap and bib and its dark gray wing and tail.
the-markings.end: The bird now wears a bold black cap and bib around its white cheek, with a smooth slate-gray wing and pointed tail.

the-feathers.for: This stage flicks in feathers so the bird looks soft, and brightens the chest where the sun catches it.
the-feathers.end: The bird looks soft and feathery, with separate wing feathers and a chest that glows creamy white in the sunlight.

the-face-and-feet.for: This stage brings the bird to life with its eye, beak and gripping feet, and one tiny spark of light in the eye.
the-face-and-feet.end: The finished painting: a bright-eyed chickadee grips its sunlit branch among hanging leaves and glowing autumn woods.
